Aśokavana
(‘the grove of अशोक trees’)
------------------------------------------
See under AŚOKA. See also RĀMĀYAṆA and SĪTĀ.

Aśoka
------------------------------------------
The third emperor of the Mauryan dynasty and one of the greatest that India has produced, अशोक ruled during the period 272—232 B. C. His empire extended from गान्धार (Afghanistan) up to southern Karnataka. The terrible bloodshed witnessed during his conquest of the कलिङ्ग Kingdom (Orissa) brought about a big change in his mental attitude. He thence-forward vowed to conquer by धर्म rather than by war and violence. He is believed to have embraced बुद्धिस्म् and dispatched Buddhist missionaries to several countries of the world. His rule was a golden era in Indian history. The several rock-edicts erected by him all over the country bespeak of his rule of धर्म.
Aśoka is also the name of a tree (Saraca indica) believed to be dear to शिव, and hence, considered sacred. The grove of अशोक trees is mentioned in the Rāmāyaṇa as the place where सीता was confined by the demon king रावण. Hence Hindu women over the ages have associated it with constancy and chastity, have worshipped it, as also eaten its tender buds.

Aśokāṣṭamī
------------------------------------------
Observance of festivals and sacred days is a common phenomenon in all societies that believe in and practise religion. In हिन्दुइस्म्, due to the variety and multiplicity of cults, the number of such days is legion.
Aśokāṣṭamī is one of the less known or minor festivals. It is celebrated on the eighth day (aṣṭamī) of the bright fortnight in the month of चैत्र (March-April) and the flowers of the अशोक tree (Saraca indica) have been specially recommended for worship, Goddess दुर्गा being the deity of worship. Hence the name अशोकाष्टमी. The day is considered doubly sacred if it happens to be a Wednesday with the पुनर्वसु नक्षत्र (seventh lunar mansion consisting of two स्तर्स्). On this day, housewives believe that, by eating the tiny buds of the अशोक tree they will be free from śoka or sorrow (a-śoka = free from sorrow). A bath in the ब्रह्मपुत्र river on this day is considered as very sacred, yielding the same fruit as the performance of the वाजपेय sacrifice.
See also VRATAS and UTSAVAS.
